title: First Visit, Sudden Blur

patient.name: Mdm Halimah Binte Yusof
patient.presenting_complaint: First visit, referred from polyclinic for sudden blurring of vision for the past 2 days

history.hpc: Mdm Halimah says 'My vision suddenly become blur two days ago, I never see like that before.' This is her first visit to SNEC, referred from the polyclinic. She is anxious. She refuses to do the near vision test, saying 'Cannot lah, I cannot see properly, no point.' You are required to perform the Patient & Family Assessment and Education and Fall Risk assessment, distance visual acuity and IOP measurement, and to recognise that sudden visual loss needs to be flagged.
history.pmhx: First visit — history to be taken. Walks in slowly and is a little unsteady.
history.family_hx: To be elicited as part of the assessment
history.social_hx: Lives with her husband. Came to clinic by herself.

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Not assessed by the PSA — for doctor review
examination_findings.fundus: Not assessed by the PSA — for doctor review

investigations.pfaer: Patient and Family Assessment and Education completed: orientation to clinic, identification of needs, and explanation of what to expect; documented appropriately
investigations.fall_risk: Fall risk screen completed — patient is unsteady on her feet and is a new, anxious, visually impaired elderly patient; identified as higher fall risk, safety measures put in place
investigations.distance_va_method: Modified LogMAR distance VA performed with the patient's usual correction; pinhole offered
investigations.near_vision: Patient declined near vision testing — declination documented and respected after explanation
investigations.iop_method: Non-contact tonometry performed after explaining the air puff

diagnosis: Patient and Family Assessment and Education and fall risk screening completed and documented; the patient is identified as a higher fall risk and safety measures are applied. Distance visual acuity shows markedly reduced right eye vision (6/60) with sudden onset over 2 days, and IOP is within normal limits. The sudden, significant unilateral visual loss is recognised as needing prompt escalation to the nurse/doctor rather than routine queueing. Near vision testing was declined and this was documented. The PSA does not make a medical diagnosis.

immediate: Confirm patient identity with two identifiers and orient the new patient to the clinic (PFAER)
Complete the fall risk screen; given unsteadiness and visual impairment, apply fall precautions (e.g. assist with walking, alert staff, appropriate seating)
Explain each test in simple language and gain cooperation; respect and document the patient's refusal of near vision after explaining its purpose
Measure distance visual acuity using the modified LogMAR method with usual correction, offer pinhole, and record both eyes accurately
Perform non-contact tonometry after explaining the air puff, and record IOP for both eyes
Recognise the sudden reduced vision (6/60, onset 2 days) as a red flag and escalate promptly to the nurse/doctor
Document all findings, the fall risk level and the near-vision declination clearly
follow_up: Flag the sudden unilateral visual loss for prioritised doctor review
Ensure fall precautions remain in place while the patient is in the clinic
Hand over assessment findings clearly to the nurse/doctor
patient_education: Reassure the anxious patient and explain what each assessment is for
Explain why sudden blurring needs to be seen promptly and that she should not leave before review
Advise on fall safety within the clinic (e.g. ask for help when walking)

key_points: Confirms identity and completes patient & family assessment and education for a new patient
Completes a fall risk screen and identifies the patient as higher risk
Explains tests clearly and respects/documents the refusal of near vision after explanation
Elicits the sudden onset (2 days) of the visual symptom
Performs modified LogMAR distance VA correctly with usual correction and offers pinhole
Records visual acuity for both eyes accurately
Performs non-contact tonometry correctly after explaining the air puff
Recognises sudden markedly reduced unilateral vision as a red flag needing escalation
Does not attempt a medical diagnosis — escalates to nurse/doctor
Understands the purpose of PFAER and fall risk assessment
Identifies the patient as higher fall risk and applies precautions
Applies fall precautions appropriate to an unsteady, visually impaired patient
Escalates the sudden visual loss promptly rather than routine queueing
Documents VA, IOP, fall risk and the near-vision declination clearly
Reassures and educates the anxious new patient
